venturebeat.com/security/the-three-layer.excerpt: Presented by Nutanix Autonomous systems that can reason, make their own decisions, and execute actions across an environment introduce a category of risk that application-level controls were never built to contain. Treating that risk as a single problem produces incomplete architectures, says Oscar Wahlberg, senior director of product management at Nutanix. "The guardrails to catch a malicious prompt won't stop an agent from hallucinating and doing something it never should have done, like accidentally deleting databases or leaking sensitive data with a credential it was granted but then uses for something entirely different," Wahlberg says. "That's the central problem as enterprises move autonomous agents out of experimentation and into production." Once an agentic system is granted execution privileges across the data center, the security posture has to scale into a defense-in-depth architecture spanning infrastructure, storage, compute, networking, and a governing control plane. Each layer addresses a distinct category of risk, rather than duplicating the same controls across the stack. No single security control or vendor can provide that protection on its own. Defense-in-depth depends on those layers working together. By dividing the responsibilities across the stack and adhering to zero trust segmentation, organizations can create a secure framework that improves their overall posture. Understanding which risks belong in each layer is what turns the principle of defense-in-depth into a practical security framework, with three layers that each have a distinct responsibility. venturebeat.com/orchestration/meta-resea.excerpt: Consider an AI agent tasked with a complex enterprise workflow like migrating massive batches of customer records from a legacy CRM to a cloud database. The agent cannot rely solely on its internal context window for a job spanning hours and depends on the runtime layer, aka the harness . This harness provides execution feedback, like server logs, to help the agent maintain an accurate understanding of dynamic API connections. It also provides state trackers and control-flow mechanisms to manage completed and pending subgoals, ensuring the agent doesn't skip or duplicate data batches. When unexpected errors occur, such as a database rejecting a batch due to strict API rate limits, the harness provides tools and instructions to help the agent recover. The main way to tell an agent how and when to use its tools is to have a human developer write a set of rules and instructions telling it what to do step-by-step. For example, a developer might instruct the agent to always search the company wiki before writing an email. Because the agent is just following a rigid script, it lacks true autonomy. It hasn't been trained to independently weigh the costs and benefits of its actions. To solve this, researchers at Meta AI and University of Illinois Urbana–Champaign introduce EvoHarness-RL , a framework that adds a layer of abstraction to the agent's harness and teaches the underlying model when to read, update, or consolidate the information it obtains from its environment. In long-horizon tasks, how AI agents read and process the information they obtain from their environment is pivotal to their success. The agent must update its understanding of its environment, track completed and pending subgoals, recover from failed actions, and reuse procedures from previous experience. "Document parsing isn't solved because the hard part isn't reading text, it's preserving structure and meaning," Nils Reimers, VP of AI Search at Cohere, told VentureBeat. "Enterprise documents mix tables, diagrams, charts, and formatting that change the interpretation of the data. Most tools still drop structure or hallucinate content, and even frontier models break on layout‑heavy pages." macrumors.com/2026/08/28/steve-jobs-scie.excerpt: A science project that Apple co-founder Steve Jobs built for his 8th-grade science fair sold at auction for $34,375. Jobs was attending Cupertino Jr. High when he designed the project, which is titled "What is the SCR?" The lot includes a display board built from plywood with three explanatory panels and a 10-page report with the same title. The left panel has a wooden model of a "typical silicon-controlled rectifier with its four alternate layers of P- and N-Type semiconductor material," while the center test circuits demonstrate the basic principles and characteristics of the silicon-controlled rectifier, as well as how it is most widely used. The right panel has a diagram and description of a 25-amp silicon-controlled rectifier. The project is labeled with Jobs' name, and the accompanying report is titled "What is the Silicon-Controlled Rectifier by Steve Jobs, Science, Mrs. Yakel, Feb. 29, 1968." A note included on the project instructs judges to plug in Circuit II and the oscilloscope to see it operate, and it asks them to "please unplug!" the device after testing it. Jobs' science fair project came from John Chovanec, Jobs' stepbrother. Chovanec's mother, Marilyn, married Paul Jobs in 1990 and continued to live in the Jobs family home in Los Altos. After Paul Jobs died in 1993, Steve Jobs declined to collect some of his personal belongings that remained in the home. Chovanec apparently asked Jobs to collect the items several times and at one point said he would keep the items himself instead. "Fine, but I don't want to be bothered about it again," Jobs reportedly responded. Chovanec previously sold other items from Jobs' early years, including posters, magazines, bow ties, a desk, and more. A 1977 Apple Computer poster sold for $659,900, while an Apple–1 Byte Shop wooden case owned by Jobs sold for $254,375. The bow ties sold for $113,580. MacBook Pro (14‑inch) and 24‑inch iMac are slated for M6 updates in late 2026.
Apple will skip M6 Pro and M6 Max, accelerating the launch of M7 Pro and M7 Max in 2027.
High‑end models like the rumored MacBook Ultra will retain M5 Pro/Max until the M7 family arrives.
The M6 features a 12‑core CPU, 12‑core GPU with ray‑tracing, and up to 170 GB/s memory bandwidth.

google_ai_search_summary_expansion.headline: Google pushes search results deeper with auto‑expanding AI Overviews
google_ai_search_summary_expansion.summary: Google now auto‑expands AI Overviews for certain queries, moving the traditional list of links farther down the page and adding an Ask Anything box.
highlights: Full AI Overview appears at the top without a "Show more" prompt
An "Ask Anything" input box is placed directly below the AI Overview
Google says expansion stops if users begin scrolling to preserve reading position
The auto‑expand trigger is inconsistent, with queries like "best game on switch 2" often activating it

court_ruling_pentagon_ban.headline: Federal Court Blocks Pentagon Ban on Anthropic’s Claude AI Model
court_ruling_pentagon_ban.summary: A U.S. District Court ruled the Pentagon’s attempt to prohibit the use of Anthropic’s Claude model illegal, overturning the ban imposed by the Trump administration.
highlights: Judge Rita Lin declared the ban “illegal and baseless”
The Defense Department had labeled Anthropic a supply‑chain risk in 2025
Anthropic sued in March and the court dismissed the Pentagon’s legal arguments
The ruling notes Anthropic lacks any backdoor access to its technology

1b_debt_ai_chips.headline: Lambda secures $1 B debt to buy Nvidia AI chips for Microsoft
1b_debt_ai_chips.summary: Lambda, the AI‑cloud firm, raised a $1 billion short‑term loan to purchase Nvidia GB300 GPUs that it will lease to Microsoft, accelerating its revenue pipeline.
highlights: Lambda obtained a $1 billion private debt facility arranged by JP Morgan Chase
The loan will fund acquisition of Nvidia GB300 GPUs for a Microsoft lease contract
Lambda previously closed a $1 billion credit facility and a $926 million loan for GPU infrastructure
The company is eyeing a $3 billion pre‑IPO financing round

glm_5_3_release.headline: Z.ai Unveils GLM‑5.3 Weights Under Restrictive $10 B Revenue License

roman_telescope_launch.summary: After overcoming funding hurdles and a name change, the telescope begins a three‑month trek to L2 to conduct unprecedented cosmic surveys.
highlights: Field of view is 100 times larger than Hubble’s, enabling 1,000‑fold faster sky surveys.
Equipped with a 300‑megapixel infrared camera and Coronagraph system for direct exoplanet imaging.
Will perform 3D scans and gravitational lensing measurements to map dark matter distribution.
Targets the second Sun‑Earth Lagrange point (L2) for a stable, deep‑space observing platform.
roman_telescope_launch.content_excerpt: after funding struggles and a name change, the nancy grace roman space telescope has been successfully launched. it will now make a three-month, one-million-mile journey to its orbit at the second sun-earth lagrange point l2 beyond the moon. the nancy grace roman space telescope launches to study dark matter and dark energy the telescope will survey our universe 1,000 times faster than hubble. from this vantage point, roman will conduct an unprecedented survey of the universe. its field of view is 100 times larger than hubble s and, according to nasa, it can survey the sky 1,000 times faster using its 300-megapixel infrared camera. roman also has a coronagraph system that can block and mask glare from stars, allowing it to directly image exoplanets, even smaller, older, and colder planets orbiting close to their stars. roman will also conduct detailed 3d scans to help map the distribution of dark matter and narrow down the potential candidates for its makeup. using the same 3d scans and gravitational lensing measurements, roman will attempt to map how dark energy shaped the evolution of the universe. nicky fox, associate administrator for the science mission directorate at nasa, said in a press release that roman will be a discovery machine that will bring us closer than ever before to answering humanity s most profound questions about our cosmic history.
